extracted.intended_audience: advertisers, journalists, and students interested in 19th-century/print advertising practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative commentary on producing effective print advertising (newspapers, posters, hoardings, kiosques) with examples from Paris, London, and other international markets; includes tactics, formats, and pitfalls. Useful for designing or assessing historical and traditional print ad campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / continual invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising constantly produces something new; no discovered expedient is final — 'there seems to be always something new springing up'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovative or novel expedients attract attention; expect rapid obsolescence of 'latest' tricks. Use novelty to arrest attention but be prepared for short-lived impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation guarantee and cost-effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers value guaranteed circulation numbers and the economics of distribution (example: the Scotchman guarantees circulation of five thousand copies for his twenty-four-sheet letter-paper scheme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure value by guaranteed reach and compare advertiser cost vs produced circulation and production costs; schemes promising circulation should be checked against implied costs (stamps, printing) and realistic pickup/sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived value and price credibility of free papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Free or giveaway advertisement sheets risk being perceived as worthless — 'it is hard to make advertisers believe that it is worth while paying for a notice in a paper which is itself not worth paying for' — such journals either 'got a price fixed on themselves, or died'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a wholly free model unless you can demonstrate independent value; perceived value influences advertiser willingness to pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory compliance and format mandates
rubrics_metrics.description: Local laws may mandate specific formats or stamps for public announcements (example: French law requires a ten-centime stamp on public announcements; posters/placards must be printed on coloured paper, Government reserves a white affiche).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design ads to comply with local regulations and to exploit any distinctive officially permitted formats (or restrictions) rather than risking fines or censorship; use mandated formats for visibility when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neatness, maintenance and currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Parisians maintain neat, fresh posters and kiosques — no 'rain-soaked bills peeling off' — making presentation and up-to-date replacement a feature of effective outdoor advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep displays fresh, well-maintained and current; poor physical upkeep undermines message credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium & placement selection (hoardings, kiosques, columns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different physical media (hoardings, 'spectacle' columns, kiosques, theatrical programme-columns) serve distinct functions and rates of renewal; e.g., theatre programmes are renewed daily and are remunerative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose placement based on audience flow and renewal frequency; high-turnover placements (theatre columns) can be lucrative; consider visibility, turnover and audience match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size/format impact (broadside vs small notices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadside advertisements (sprawling capitals, sometimes covering half a page) have strong visual impact but may be considered 'ugly' by some audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use large-format ads for spectacle/impact but weigh aesthetic and audience sensibilities; match format to brand tone and target readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stealth/advertorial effectiveness — 'looks less like what it is'
rubrics_metrics.description: An advertisement 'is more valuable in proportion as it looks less like what it really is' — editorial puffs and reclames disguised as journalism are actively sought after in some markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtle advertorials and content-marketing that read like editorial can be highly effective; ensure ethical and legal boundaries are observed and balance subtlety with clear calls to action where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enigmatical/curiosity-driven advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Using mystery or enigmatic forms ('Opoponax' mystery) arouses public curiosity and can be imitated successfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ teasers and enigmatic messaging to provoke curiosity and dialogue, but plan follow-up to convert curiosity into sales; originality matters to sustain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimonials and quoted authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Long columns of testimonials and celebrity/paper names (Brinsmead's use of Sir Julius Benedict, Brinley Richards, etc.) are used to imply quality, though some quotations may be inauthentic or anachronistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genuine, verifiable testimonials and endorsements; beware of misattributing or overstating endorsements (anti-pattern: quoting deceased figures or irrelevant authorities undermines credibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect advertising / memory anchors
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect mentions (e.g., a line in a paper or a small pasted notice about a play) can fix an address or name in a reader's memory and drive future visits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate brand mentions into contexts (theatre, social columns) where readers will repeatedly encounter and remember the name; subtle repetition builds recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional freebies and branded novelties
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributing balloons, fans, illuminated tickets, and other small branded items (as in Paris: air balloons, fans, illuminated cards) attracts public attention and keeps the name visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tasteful, well-designed freebies that target customers and create repeated brand exposure; ensure items reflect brand quality to avoid cheapening image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of controversy/censorship as publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Proclaiming that a work was 'forbidden' (censorship) in a given venue has been used to create notoriety and boost sales (example: 'la Censure a interdit 'Pailotte'...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversy can be leveraged for publicity but carries reputational risk; plan for potential backlash and assess whether notoriety will convert to desired outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place/locale as quality signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Localities are used to typify quality (e.g., 'Mayfair Sherry' suggests high tone and elegant bottling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use place-based branding when legitimate; ensure claims tied to locale are accurate to avoid charges of misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience targeting and message tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Different ad specimens are tailored to specific audiences (examples: advertisements 'intended for the ladies', matrimonial notices, stomachics, women's fashions), each with distinct tone and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences and craft messages, claims, and formats appropriate to each segment's values and interests; use language, benefits and visuals that resonate with the intended group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of theatrical/celebrity mentions and paid puffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Managers and performers often use mentions in pantomime or press to paraded shops or goods; entertainers were historically solicited to mention products publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider paid mentions or product placement in performances and cultural outputs, but manage authenticity and disclose commercial relationships where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding heavy-handed 'puff-pars' — subtlety over clumsy praise
rubrics_metrics.description: British 'puff-pars' were often clumsy compared with refined French reclames; the 'cloven foot' shows under too-obvious wrappers of praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for cultivated, artful promotion rather than overwrought, obviously self-serving language; subtlety preserves credibility and can be more persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale, repetition and frequency (programme renewals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily-renewed columns (theatre programmes) and repeated presence across hoardings and papers (some firms aim to be on every hoarding) drive visibility and familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan frequency and repetition across selected media to build recognition; sustained presence often outperforms one-off large splashes for long-term recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear response mechanism and contact details
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ads included explicit addresses, response stamps ('Timbres pour reponse'), prices and locations to facilitate replies and purchases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always include a clear, convenient call-to-action and contact/response mechanism appropriate to the medium (reply stamps, addresses, theatres, shops).

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization, language correctness and cultural sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples from foreign ports and papers (bad English in Chinese port notices; German and Portuguese announcements) highlight translation/localization matters; mistakes can be comical or misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Localize language and cultural content correctly; avoid mistranslation and be sensitive to local norms to maintain clarity and avoid offense or ridicule.
